name: Garnet-Shallows
description: Garnet-Shallows earns its name from the ruddy tint of its world-ocean, stained a deep rose by trillions of photosynthetic microorganisms that bloom across its surface. The planet has no true continents, only chains of volcanic atolls and coral-like mineral formations that break the waterline in clusters. A faint debris ring arcs across the sky, the remnant of a shattered moon, scattering garnet-colored light at sunrise and sunset.

The warmth of the water rises through the atolls as gentle steam, giving the air a perpetual softness. Beneath the surface, vast kelp-analog forests sway in geothermal currents, their fronds producing oxygen so efficiently that the atmosphere remains remarkably fresh. The sound of the ocean is omnipresent, a rhythmic pulse that seems almost biological in its regularity.

No intelligent species has ever called Garnet-Shallows home, yet its flora has attracted centuries of pharmaceutical interest. Compounds extracted from the deep-water kelp analogs have proven effective against a range of degenerative diseases, making this world one of the most commercially valuable oceanic planets in the sector. The debris ring suggests a catastrophic lunar event in the planet's past, one that may have seeded the ocean with the rare minerals that fuel its extraordinary biology.

Harvesting rights are fiercely contested among biomedical corporations, and unlicensed collection vessels are a persistent problem. The ecosystem is robust but not infinite, and marine biologists warn that over-extraction could trigger a cascade collapse of the bloom cycle. For now, Garnet-Shallows remains a jewel of living chemistry, but the balance between profit and preservation grows more precarious each season.
